newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen government wins parliament's confidence.
newsitem.headline: Yemen government wins parliament's confidence.

text.p: Yemen's new government led by Prime Minister Faraj Said Bin Ghanem, a Polish-educated economist from the south, on Thursday won an overwhelming vote of confidence from parliament.
He gained 255 votes from 270 deputies present during the session. Four voted against him, 11 abstained and the remaining 31 in the 301-seat chamber did not show up.

President Ali Abdullah Saleh swore in Bin Ghanem, who sits as an independent, days after April 27 elections in which the ruling General People's Congress (GPC) won a landslide victory. The elections were the first since Yemen's 1994 civil war.
Bin Ghanem told deputies his government would continue economic reforms launched in 1995 in agreement with the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.
"We are keen to continue and complete economic, monetary and financial reforms," he said.
Yemen, one of the Middle East's poorest states with per capita income of just $200 a year and one of the world's fastest-growing populations, is hard pressed to tackle unemployment among the young.
Expected austerity measures and efforts to cut heavy state subsidies could also prove sensitive, some economists and diplomats say.
Bin Ghamen also promised to do his utmost to settle a 61-year-old border row with Saudi Arabia and to boost Yemen's ties with other Gulf Arab states.
Yemen and oil-rich Saudi Arabia signed a memorandum of understanding in 1995 to resolve their border dispute.

Yemen's relations with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Arab states, which were angered when Sanaa appeared to side with Iraq during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis over Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, have improved in the last few years.
